en: Preface to the *Boshan Jingyu* (Boshan’s Words of Caution):
"Jing" (caution) carries the meaning of awakening or alertness; some say it means to startle. It is like a thief spying upon a grand mansion.

The host sits in the hall by lamplight at night, making sounds with his coughs and clears. The thief, fearing exposure, cannot proceed. Yet, were he to fall even slightly into a drowsy sleep, [the disaster would follow].

Taking advantage of an opening, they enter; their bags are thus overturned. Therefore, when watchtowers strike the wooden clappers and *diaodou* gongs resound along the chariots, even if a sudden change occurs, there is no cause for alarm because precautions were taken before the trigger point.

Human beings face the great affliction of birth and death—a long dream from which they do not awaken for ten thousand kalpas—and yet they also serve as intermediaries for thieves, daily robbing the family treasures. Were it not for a hero of Great Awakening?
Painful words of admonition are necessary; otherwise, one remains drunk and dreaming for a lifetime, with no day of awakening in sight.
It is not only during sleep that one cannot master oneself; even by day, with eyes wide open, demonic speech is even more prevalent.

Therefore, Master Bosan, riding upon the power of his compassionate vows, came as a Great Physician-King to treat the maladies of madness and arrogance with the single flavor of gāthās. Thus, there is the "Instruction on Zen Illness."
The Five Chapters of Admonitions are direct, concise, and appropriate; they thoroughly expound the essential maladies within the very marrow of Zen practice.
His instructions on the methods of cultivation are most urgent and vital. This is truly a new and indispensable manual for the Zen school.
It is also the ninefold transformation of the Golden Elixir that rescues the world. Now, as for Chan: it is a provisional name without substantial essence; how could there be any affliction in it?
It is simply that many who practice Chan give rise to clinging emotions and erroneous interpretations, being deceived and destroyed by their own mind, intellect, and consciousness.

Rather than seeking within the dynamic realm of the kōan, they instead seek within intellectual understanding. They are either obstructed by the words and phrases of the ancients, or they remain stuck in stagnant water.
Drowned within; or else one sits within "armored non-action. It is not that the mind lacks sharpness, yet it cannot die;
nor is it that the mind is dull and attached, yet it cannot turn. Consequently, the life-root is difficult to sever, and birth-and-death remain vividly present.
The entire body is my own illness—it is not that Zen has an illness. At worst, this results in being falsely possessed by demons, such that even the Buddha could not save them. This is called...

This is a sickness of karma, not a sickness of Chan. Even if one attains various states of mind through death, if one is unwilling to apply oneself to practice so as to accord with the principle of the Dharmakāya, and has never stepped upon the pivotal mechanism of the higher realm, then sitting complacently and at ease within a basket of rice—this very complacency is precisely the sickness of Chan.
Thus, a monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is purity?"
The Dharmakāya, Guṇabhadra, is the source of immeasurable great illnesses. These words are like a chestnut burr; truly difficult to swallow or spit out.

The ancients, having passed through an illness from within genuine inquiry and true realization, naturally did not err when applying their hands, for they would never indiscriminately drop their needles or awls.
They required a person who had cut off the breath and recognized pain and itching before they would consent to examine them. Thus, one must recognize the illness.
Only then can one eliminate illness. To harmonize oneself before harmonizing others—can this not be called "one who has broken an arm three times becomes a skilled physician"?
Great Master Bosan has long been investigating this Way; he is profoundly versatile and integrated. Whatever words or phrases he utters strike the very core of the matter.
This is not because he intentionally employs lofty, subtle, or mysterious discourse to leave people ignorant; rather, it is because he has personally realized the truth through daily practice.
He has traversed the stages of realization; his insight, speech, conduct, and application have reached their consummation. His principles are lucid and refined, and his eloquence is unimpeded.

Thus, he speaks with such ease regarding the maladies of Chan, like one holding the jade mirror of the Qin palace, clearly reflecting the hearts and livers of all officials so that not even a hair’s breadth of concealment can remain.
Among those who have sat upon the curved-lacquered throne throughout antiquity and claimed to be *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friends) preaching Chan, none have equaled you, Master.
This is truly rare and peerless. However, the illnesses of Chan are most difficult to speak of; even if one were to speak of them, one could not exhaustively describe them all.
Why is this? Illness is the illness of the *dharmakāya*. Since the *dharmakāya* is infinite, how could its illnesses ever have an end?

One who skillfully rescues the *dharmakāya* from illness takes that very illness as a wondrous medicine, takes it as the daily meal, and takes it as a sweatshirt worn close to the skin. It lies in skillfully preserving it—while...

Thus it was. In the past, ancient masters engaged in "play" while in the midst of illness as a form of Buddha-work. This was because they had seen through the fact that the *dharmakāya* has no master;

thus, the illness cleared away of its own accord. Therefore, Dongshan said: "When the old monk looks, he does not see any illness. It arises solely from the attachment of deluded thoughts, and thus the various 'Zen illnesses' compete to arise.
Long ago, the Buddha spoke of the demonic activities regarding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, as well as those of the external paths.

Discrimination (*vikalpa*) is precisely what constitutes the maladies of meditation (*dhyāna-roga*) for people today. However, attachment to it becomes a demonic obstacle (*māra*), while discrimination is termed "external.
To neither be attached nor discriminate is likewise not yet a malady. Therefore, it is said: "Not forming a mind of superiority is called a 'wholesome state' (*kuśala-viṣaya*);

if one forms a sacred interpretation (*ārya-adhimukti*), one immediately succumbs to the various evils. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "There was a guide who well knew the paths that were passable or obstructed, and those that were perilous and difficult."

Thus, he was able to lead those multitudes forward to the place of treasure. Therefore, this treatise by the Great Master is truly a boat for the final age and a direct path for those with the initial resolve.
It will not only be beneficial for the present day, but will also provide aid for the future.

For those who resolutely wish to engage in Chan practice and cultivate their efforts to seek the gate of great enlightenment, if they are willing to examine this book closely, it will provide them with a great strategic framework.
It can cause the state where doubt has not yet arisen to give rise to it; it can penetrate the root of the illness where it has not yet been pierced.
It is like sifting through sand to reveal a jewel—one must take it for oneself. It is like parting the mist to see the sky, ensuring that people do not remain lost.
Within the path that cuts off all ways, there is a way to emerge; within the words of death, there is a phrase of life. It is like a perfect sphere rolling upon a tray, never lingering in one place.

The subtle function of speech is such as this. If every person knows how to apply their mind in this way, they can see the Way while sitting or sleeping, without wasting the money for so many straw sandals, until they reach the ground of great peace and happiness, where they breathe through the same nostrils as the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If there are those who can use this to admonish themselves and thereby admonish others, and use this to heal themselves and thereby heal others.

He may also be called the "Present-day King of Physicians," for he has caused the life-vein of the Patriarchs to flow freely and ensured that the national pulse and the pulse of wisdom are both firmly established.
Thus, it may be said that he does not fail the master’s skillful means and aspirational power in bestowing this teaching. This concludes the preface.

In the first month of autumn, the Xin Hai year of the Wanli era, the disciple Liu Chongqing of Xinzhou bows in homage and inscribes this table of contents for the *Caodong Master Boshan’s Words of Caution on Studying Chan*,
Volume One.
Instructions for Beginners on Practicing *Gongfu*: A Collection of Evaluations of Ancient Masters’ Admonitions, Volume II;
Evaluations of Ancient Masters’ Admonitions; Instructions for Resolving Doubts When They Fail to Arise: An Admonition.
Exhibiting Words for Arousing the Doubting Mind; Exhibiting Words for Warning Zen Practitioners to Investigate Kōans;
Ten Verses on Investigating Zen;
Master Boshan’s Words for Warning Zen Practice.
Compiled by Chief Seat Chengzheng:

Admonitions for Beginners on Cultivating Practice When first beginning to cultivate practice, you must first resolve to break through birth and death with firm determination. You must see through the world and the body-and-mind.

All these are merely provisional conditions; there is no real master. If you do not bring forth the great principle that is inherently possessed, then the mind of birth and death will not be shattered.
Since the mind of birth and death is not shattered, the ghost of impermanence’s slaughter does not cease for even a single thought-moment.
How, then, can this be dispelled? Take this single thought as a tile for knocking at the gate, as if sitting amidst the flames of a raging fire seeking [escape].
It emerges in a manner that resembles [the original state]. One must not take a single step erratically; one must not stop for even a single step; one must not give rise to a single separate thought;

one must not hope for another to rescue one. At such a time, you need only disregard the fierce fire, disregard your own body and life, not hope for anyone’s rescue, not give rise to other thoughts, and refuse to pause for even a moment. Charge straight ahead; if you can charge forth, you will emerge.
This is a skillful approach.
In practicing the work, the essential point lies in giving rise to the "doubting mind" (*yiqing*). What is meant by the doubting mind? It is like being born and not knowing whence one comes;
one cannot help but doubt the place of origin. It is like dying and not knowing whither one goes; one cannot help but doubt the destination. This is the pivotal crux of birth and death.
When it is shattered, doubt suddenly arises; it is knotted upon one’s brows and eyelashes, neither released nor driven away.
Suddenly, one morning, when the mass of doubt is smashed to pieces, what idle furniture are the two words "birth and death"? *Aḥ!* An ancient worthy said:
"Great doubt brings great awakening; small doubt brings small awakening; no doubt, no awakening."
In practicing the Way, affix the character for "death" upon your forehead. Treat your physical body and mind as if they were already dead;
let there be only this single thought that seeks to investigate and clarify the truth. This present moment of thought is like a long sword leaning against the sky:
if one should touch its edge, it is utterly impossible to do so; yet if one lets it stagnate or dulls it through neglect, the sword will vanish.
It has been a long time since I began my practice.
My greatest fear is becoming attached to states of stillness, which causes people to become mired in arid desolation, remaining unaware and unperceptive.
While people find active states distasteful, they rarely feel such distaste for states of stillness. This is because practitioners have habitually dwelt amidst the clamor and bustle of the world.
This state corresponds with the realm of stillness, like eating molasses or honey, or like a person exhausted from long toil who delights in sleep;
how could one know it for oneself?

Even the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who seek to extinguish body and mind and transform themselves into inert stones, likewise enter through this realm of stillness. This is truly because... [the year]... (Note: The final character "歲" appears to be a scribal error or fragment; in the context of such texts, it may relate to a date or a specific period, but as it stands, it remains untranslated.)
After many months have passed, it becomes withered and yet more withered; it becomes still and yet more still. One falls into a state of ignorance—how is this any different from wood or stone?
When people dwell in a state of quietude, they merely seek to clarify that great matter within the seam of their robes;

they do not realize that it is only within quietude that one attains it. Yet, if one seeks the characteristic of quietude within that great matter, it is utterly unattainable. This is true attainment.

Furthermore, in practicing the Way, one must be upright, centered, firm, and resolute, not conforming to worldly sentiments. If you respond according to your emotions, you will fail to make progress in your practice;
not only will you fail to progress, but as days and months pass, there is no doubt that you will simply follow the common stream of worldly teachers.
Furthermore, when a practitioner of the Way lifts their head, they do not see the sky; when they lower their head, they do not see the earth. Looking at mountains, they are not mountains;
seeing water, it is not water. Walking, they do not know they are walking; sitting, they do not know they are sitting. Among thousands or tens of thousands of people, they are not seen.
There is a person whose entire being, inside and out, is nothing but a single mass of doubt; one might say they have stirred up the entire world into a mass of doubt.
They vow not to rest until this doubt is shattered—this is the most vital point of practice.
What is meant by "stirring up the turbid world"? The great principle inherently possessed since immeasurable kalpas has been profoundly still and silent, never once moved.
It requires the person themselves to rouse their spirit; when heaven revolves and earth turns, there will naturally arise a state of experience like surging waves and billowing tides.
In practicing the Way, do not fear death but rather fear failing to attain life. Do not fear life but rather fear failing to attain death.

When the fruit and the doubt are bound together as one, turbulent circumstances need not be rejected and will naturally dissipate; the deluded mind need not be purified and will naturally become pure.
At the gateway of the six sense organs, there is naturally a state of vast openness. If you touch it, you arrive; if you call upon it, it responds.
Why worry about not being alive?
When your practice reaches its peak, it is like carrying a thousand-jin load that one cannot set down even if one wished; it is like seeking something of vital importance.
It is like searching for a lost object. If you do not find it, do not cease your efforts; however, within that process, you must not give rise to attachment, clinging, or conceptualization.

Attachment becomes illness, clinging becomes a demon, and conceptualization becomes the external. If you can attain single-mindedness and one-pointedness—just like searching for a lost object—then these three will dissolve and no longer intersect.
That is to say, the moment the mind arises or a thought moves, you have already deviated.
This is the essence of the Dharma.
When applying yourself to practice, when you raise the *huatou*, it must be vivid and clear, like a cat stalking a mouse.
As the ancients said, "I shall not rest until I have slain Li Nu. Otherwise, you will sit in a ghost cave, muddled and drowsy.
To spend a lifetime in such a state—what benefit is there?
When a cat catches a mouse, it stares with wide-open eyes and braces its four paws; it will not rest until the mouse is in its mouth.
Even if chickens or dogs are nearby, it has no leisure to look at them. A practitioner of Zen is just like this—it is nothing but a state of intense, resolute indignation.
One must clearly understand this principle: even if the eight sensory objects were to intersect before one, there would be no leisure to look back;
should a stray thought arise, not only will the mouse escape, but the cat itself will run away as well.

When practicing the Way for a single day, one must see the work accomplished in that very day. If one proceeds with negligence and indolence, there will be no end to it for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
At that time, Boshan would insert a single stick of incense; as soon as he saw the incense, he would say:
"The practice remains as before, neither diminished nor increased. How many sticks of incense are used in a single day? How many sticks of incense are used in a year?"
It is further said: "The passing of time and light is swift; the seasons do not wait for man. Before the Great Matter is clarified, when will it ever be resolved?
Thinking thus with deep regret, one should apply oneself with even greater diligence.
When practicing cultivation, one must not speculate upon the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients or attempt to provide arbitrary interpretations.
Even if one were to grasp each and every word through such understanding, it would have no connection to oneself.

One fails to realize that every word and every phrase of the ancients is like a great mass of fire: one cannot approach it, nor can one touch it; how much less can one sit or lie within it? Furthermore, regarding...
Within this, some are divided into the great and the small; some discourse on the superior and others on the inferior. Those who do not lose their bodies or forfeit their lives are but few.

This matter does not accord with the vehicles of the teachings (śāsana-yāna); thus, even those who have long practiced the Mahāyāna do not know or recognize it, let alone the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the various Small Vehicles.
How could the Three Worthies and Ten Sages not be conversant with the teachings? Yet, regarding this one [truth], they speak...
This matter strikes terror into the hearts of those of the Three Vehicles and sends the souls of the Ten Stages trembling.

Even Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, who preach the Dharma like clouds and rain and deliver inconceivable numbers of sentient beings, causing them to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), are still said to possess "ignorance regarding the knowable" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha*); they are entirely out of harmony with the Way.
How much more so, then, for those below them? For this matter, from the stage of an ordinary person, is suddenly identical to the essence of the Buddha; it is that which people...
It is difficult to believe. Those who believe are vessels; those who do not believe are not vessels. All practitioners who wish to enter this vehicle of the Dharma must enter through faith.
This single word "faith" has both shallow and deep dimensions, and both false and correct aspects; it must be discerned. As for the shallow:
when anyone enters a gateway to the Dharma, who would say they do not believe? Yet they merely believe in the gateway of the Dharma, rather than believing in their own mind. As for the deep: all...
Even Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas may not yet possess full faith. As the *Huayan shu* states:

"To perceive one who can preach the Dharma and a multitude who listen to the Dharma is still not to have entered the gate of faith. If it is said that "the very mind is Buddha," who would say they do not believe?
When it comes to being asked, "Are you the Buddha?", one resorts to evasive defenses and fails to take full responsibility. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Though they exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Why is there such a mind that exhausts its thoughts to measure?
It is simply because faith is not complete.
Regarding the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox: that one's own mind is itself the Buddha is called "right faith. To seek dharmas outside of the mind is called "heterodox faith.
One must thoroughly investigate and clarify that the Buddha is precisely one's own mind, practicing it personally until reaching a state of non-doubt; only then is it called right faith.

For instance, if one is vague and superficial, merely guessing that the three [terms] are similar and simply saying "mind is Buddha" without truly recognizing one's own mind, this is indeed called heterodox.
Faith.
In antiquity, when one picked peaches, one was settled; when one tilled the soil, one was settled; even while performing manual labor, one was settled.

How could this be a state of concentration (*samādhi*) achieved only by sitting for a long time, suppressing and restraining the mind so that it does not arise? If it were so, it would be called "perverse concentration" (*mithyā-samādhi*), not true concentration.
The practitioner must maintain right intention.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "The Nāga is always in samādhi; there is no time when it is not in samādhi. One must penetrate and see the fundamental substance before one can correspond with this samādhi.
Thus did Śākyamuni descend from Tuṣita Heaven, enter the imperial palace, go into the Snowy Mountains, and behold the morning star.
He opens the assembly of illusions. Without emerging from this samādhi, otherwise one would be swept away and drowned by moving objects;
how then could it be called "samādhi"? Within moving objects, the place of arising cannot be found; within still objects, the place of arising likewise cannot be found.
Since there is no place of arising in either movement or stillness, what can serve as an object? If you realize this meaning, it is all simply the single substance of samādhi.
It fills and pervades everywhere, leaving no residual aggregates behind.
When practicing the Way, one must not be stained by worldly dharmas; even a single drop of attachment to the Buddha-dharma is not permitted.

How much more so regarding worldly dharmas? If the true critical phrase (*huatou*) manifests before you, you will walk upon ice without perceiving cold, tread upon fire without perceiving heat, and pass straight through a thicket of thorns with your body stretched across it, without perceiving any obstruction.

Only then can you move freely and directly through the midst of worldly affairs. Otherwise, you will be entirely turned about by external conditions; if you wish for your practice to reach completion, [you must do as described].
A fragment. Even in a donkey’s year, one has not yet dreamed of such a thing.

When practicing the work of cultivation, one must not seek out the literal text or follow along with every phrase; to merely memorize words and sayings is not only useless, it creates obstacles for the practice.
True cultivation would instead turn into discursive conceptualization (*prapañca*). If you wish for the mind’s movements to be cut off, how could this possibly be achieved?
Is it so? In practicing the Way, one fears most the use of conceptual inference (*anumāna*). To force the mind to settle upon an object is to distance oneself further from the Way;
even if you practice until Maitreya descends to be born, you will surely find no connection. But for one in whom the great doubt (*sīmānta*) suddenly arises, it fills the void of space.
One does not realize there is even the name "empty space. It is as if one were sitting amidst silver mountains and iron walls;
one simply must find a way out. If one cannot find a way out, how can one attain peace and stability?
Just proceed in this manner, and when the time comes, there will naturally be a decisive resolution.

Recently, there have been certain heterodox teachers who teach students that one need not apply oneself to spiritual practice (*kung-fu*). They even claim that the ancients never engaged in such practice.
These words are most poisonous; they delude and mislead the younger generation, leading them straight into hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Chan Master Dayi’s *Inscription on Seated Meditation* says: "By all means, do not say that the Way does not require study;
the ancient sages were diligent as their guiding compass. Although it is an old hall and a field of leisure, have you ever truly won it back?

If one claims to have attained the principle without needing to investigate through study, this person is a "Maitreya born by nature" and a "Śākyamuni by spontaneity. Such individuals are called "acceptable."

O you who claim to have compassion! It is likely that you yourself have never engaged in genuine investigation. Perhaps, upon seeing an ancient master’s single question and answer, you attained a superficial realization;
you then interpreted it through the lens of your own conscious intellect and began deceiving others with it. Eventually, you may even contract a severe fever.
Crying out in agony to the heavens—something you will never need during your lifetime. Yet, when the time comes for your life to end, you will be like a crab dropped into a boiling pot;
with hands flailing and feet scrambling, what use will it be to regret? How could such remorse avail?
Master Huangbo said: "When worldly toil is utterly cast off, the matter is extraordinary; one must firmly grasp the rope's end to carry out this task.
Were it not for a single experience of bone-chilling cold, how could one attain the fragrance of plum blossoms that numbs the nose? These words are most intimate and direct.
If you use this verse to exhort yourself at all times, your practice will naturally progress. It is like a journey of a hundred *li*: having traveled one...
If you take a step, you fall short by one; if you do not walk, simply remain right here.
Even if you can explain the affairs of your village with perfect clarity, in the end you have not arrived home. How could that ever suffice for the ultimate matter?

In practicing the Way, the character *qiè* (to apply oneself earnestly) is of the utmost importance. This character carries the greatest power; without such earnest application, one falls into indolence.
If one gives rise to indolence, then one will become negligent and unrestrained, reaching no bounds. If one applies the mind with earnest sincerity, how could negligence and indolence possibly arise?
One should know that with this single word "earnest," there is no reason why one cannot reach the ground of the ancients.
If one does not fear birth and death and yet fails to break through the mind, abandoning this essential word to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere, one is entirely deluded and running outside the path;
how could such practice be considered equal to the work of *gongfu*?
The single word "cut" (qie) not only eliminates faults; it immediately transcends the three natures of good, evil, and the indeterminate.

With this single phrase as the *huatou*, if one applies the mind with great intensity, one does not think of good; if one applies the mind with great intensity, one does not think of evil; if one applies the mind with great intensity, one does not fall into the indeterminate.
When the *huatou* is intense, there is no agitation; when the *huatou* is intense, there is no dullness. The *huatou*...
When manifest before one, it does not fall into the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The single character "qie" (intimate) is a word of profound intimacy. When the application of mind is intimate, there are no gaps; therefore, demons cannot enter.
When the application of mind is intimate, one does not give rise to conceptual calculations of existence, non-existence, and so forth; thus, one does not fall into the ranks of the heterodox paths.

When one applies oneself to the practice, one does not know walking when walking, nor sitting when sitting. This is because the "critical phrase" (huatou) has appeared before one, yet the doubt has not been resolved;
at such a time, one is not even aware of the existence of body and mind, let alone whether one is walking or sitting.

In practicing the Way, one most fears the tendency toward discursive thought regarding the composition of poetry, gāthās, or prose essays. If one’s poetry or gāthās are perfected, one is called a "poet-monk";
if one’s prose essays are skillful, one is termed a "literary monk. These have no connection whatsoever to the practice of Chan meditation.

Whenever encountering circumstances that are adverse or favorable, which stir the movements of the mind, one must immediately awaken to them; one should seize the *huatou* (critical phrase) and not allow oneself to be turned by external conditions.
"Only then can it be attained. Some say, "It does not matter if one does not strike. These three characters are most misleading; students must examine them carefully.

Those who practice meditation often fear falling into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). When the *huatou* (critical phrase) is present before one, how could there be any emptiness? It is precisely this fear of falling into...
If one cannot even empty the mind when it is already empty, how much less can one bring the *huatou* (critical phrase) to presence?
When practicing the work, if the doubt-mind (*yiqing*) is not resolved, one must feel as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss or treading upon thin ice.

To lose mindfulness for even a hair’s breadth is to lose one's body and life. Because the doubt-mind is not resolved, the Great Principle remains unclarified. Furthermore, when the single breath does not return...
In this life, one is led by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), unable to avoid following the consciousness as it departs according to karma; one changes head and face, unaware and unknowing.
Because of this, doubt upon doubt is added. One must take up the *huatou* (critical phrase): if it is not clear, one must resolutely seek clarity;
if it is not broken through, one must resolutely seek its breakthrough. It is like catching a thief: one must see the stolen goods before the task is accomplished.
In practicing the Way, you must not harbor a mind that awaits enlightenment. It is like a person traveling on a road who stays upon the path waiting for home to arrive;
they will never reach home. You must simply walk until you arrive. If you harbor a mind that awaits enlightenment, you will never awaken.
You must simply press forward until enlightenment is attained. When great awakening occurs, it is like a lotus suddenly blooming, or like waking from a great dream. This is because of the dream.
Awakening does not wait for awakening; it awakens itself when one is in deep sleep. A flower cannot be made to bloom by force; it blooms naturally when the season arrives.

Likewise, enlightenment does not wait for enlightenment; it awakens itself when causes and conditions converge. When I say "when causes and conditions converge," the essential point lies in the earnestness of the *huatou* (critical phrase).

One must press and constrain oneself until awakening occurs—it is certainly not a matter of waiting for awakening. Furthermore, the moment of awakening is like parting the clouds to see the sky, vast and open.
Without support. Heaven revolves and earth turns; it is yet another transformation of the realm.
In practicing the Way, one must be urgent and correct; one must be continuous and subtle; one must be harmonious and expansive. What is meant by "urgency"? One's life depends on each breath.
Before the Great Matter is clarified, if a single breath does not return, the path ahead will be vast and empty, and one will not know where one is going. One cannot afford to be lax.

"Not tight. An ancient worthy said: "It is like a hemp rope that, when soaked in water, becomes tighter with every step. What is meant by 'correct'? A student must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma.
Among the three thousand seven hundred patriarchs, there are many precedents; if there is a discrepancy even as small as a hair’s breadth," [the error is grave].
One then enters a deviant path. As the Sūtra says: "This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. What is meant by "dense and seamless"?
It is where the eyebrows and empty space are joined together, such that a needle cannot pierce them and water cannot moisten them; there is not even the slightest gap to be found.
If there were even a hair’s breadth of a gap, then demonic realms would seize that opening to enter. An ancient worthy said: "In a single moment..."
It is not present; it is like a dead person. What is meant by "fusing and opening"? If the world is one zhang wide, then the ancient mirror is one zhang wide.
If the ancient mirror is one zhang wide, then the brazier is one zhang wide. It is never restricted or fixed to remaining in a single place.
Grasp firmly the head of the dead snake; do not let it hang down at both ends. Vast and expansive! As the ancient masters said:

"Perfectly identical to the great void, lacking nothing and having no excess. When one truly reaches this state of profound openness, one sees neither body nor mind within, nor does one see the world without;
only then does one find the point of entry.
If it is tense but not correct, one will labor in vain; if it is correct but not tense, one cannot enter.
Once entered, it must be continuous and subtle before it can become responsive. Once it is responsive, it must be fused and expansive to constitute the realm of transformation.

In practicing the Way, one must not allow even a single thread of extraneous thought to enter. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one should single-mindedly maintain the original koan (huatou) and give rise to a state of doubt.
One must strive with intense resolve to reach a definitive conclusion.

If there is even a trace of extraneous thought, as the ancients said, "poisonous weeds have entered the heart"; this will not only harm one's physical life, but it will damage one's life of wisdom. This is what students must heed.
One must not fail to be cautious.
What I call "separate thoughts" applies not only to worldly matters; within the Buddha-dharma, everything other than the ultimate investigation of the mind is termed a separate thought.
Furthermore, this applies not only to matters within the Buddha-dharma, but even to the act of grasping at or rejecting anything upon the substance of the mind itself.
"Grasping it and transforming it—these are all merely discursive thoughts.
When a practitioner says, "I cannot practice," one should simply practice on the basis of that very inability.
It is like a person who does not know the way: they must simply seek the path. One cannot say, "Since I cannot find the path, I shall stop. For if one finds the path...
It lies in practice. Only when you have reached home can it be so. You must not stand on the road without moving;
otherwise, there will never be a day you reach home.

Practice the work. Practice until you reach the place where there is nowhere for the mind to apply itself, the place of the ten-thousand-fathom precipice, the place where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves, and the place where the patterns intertwine and the angles converge.
It is like a rat entering a cow’s horn; there will naturally be a decisive breakthrough.
In practicing the work, the most feared thing is a clever mind. A clever mind is a medicinal taboo;

if one violates it by even the slightest degree, then even if the true medicine appears before them, it cannot save them. If one is truly a Chan practitioner, their eyes are like those of the blind and their ears like those of the deaf;
as soon as a thought arises, it is as if they have run headlong into a silver mountain and an iron wall. Thus it is.
Only then will one's practice begin to accord with the Way.
When the practice is performed with such sincerity and earnestness that one’s body and mind, as well as the external world, are refined until they resemble iron stakes, [the goal is achieved].
One must simply wait for it to burst and break apart; furthermore, one must gather it back together before the work of cultivation can be perfected.
One need not fear making mistakes; one only fears not recognizing them as such.

Even if one happens to walk upon a mistaken path, if one is willing to recognize that error in a single thought-moment, this is the very foundation for becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch and the essential highway for transcending birth and death. It is the means to shatter Māra.
The bottom of the net is a sharp tool. The Great Master Śākyamuni verified each and every point of the non-Buddhist teachings as being erroneous;
he simply did not sit within their conceptual traps. One should know that this is the meaning of the four characters "non-abiding" (wúzhù).

From the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to the rank of a Great Sage, this principle applies not only to the supramundane Dharma, but even in the mundane world, where there may be moments of forgetfulness, it requires nothing more than this.
If you recognize your error and abandon it immediately, you can become a pure and upright person.
However, if you cling stubbornly to your mistake as being right and refuse to acknowledge your error, then even if a living Buddha appears before you, he cannot save you.
In practicing the Way, one must not avoid clamor to seek stillness, nor close the eyes and shut them tight to make a living within a ghost cave.

As the ancients said, "Sitting beneath the Black Mountain" or "sinking in dead water"—what use is this for the ultimate matter? One must simply be able to practice amidst circumstances and conditions;
only then is it a place where true strength is gained. A single phrase of the *huatou* should be placed directly upon one's brow.
Whether walking or sitting, whether dressing or eating, or welcoming guests and attending to visitors—what is required is simply to clarify where this one phrase-head (huatou) lands.
One day, while washing one's face, one will touch one’s own nose and realize it was all along too near; thus, one attains a state of effortless ease.
Exerting effort in practice, one fears that recognizing the divine constitutes a mere Buddhist ritual; thus, one may raise the eyebrows, blink the eyes, shake the head, or turn the brain.

One might think there is something particularly extraordinary about this; yet, if you take the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) as the true reality, you will not even be fit to be a servant to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

In practicing the work of cultivation, it is precisely required that the sphere of mental activity be extinguished. You must by no means attempt to settle the mind through conceptualization, such as pondering over or engaging in questions and answers regarding spiritual encounters (*kaiyuan*).
Dongshan said: "If the essence is subtle, the fundamental source is lost; if the function is obscure, the beginning and end are forgotten—one then becomes unfit for conversation."

When great realization is attained, each and every samādhi flows forth from one's own mind; as for the contemplation and cultivation [thereof], how could it possibly be compared [to the previous state]—it is like the difference between heaven and earth!
In one's practice, do not fear that one cannot reach the goal; the very effort to reach what has not been reached is itself the practice. As the ancient masters said:
This is the gate of liberation that has no gate; it is the intention of the Way-person that has no intention. Its value lies in thoroughly comprehending the point of entry.
If you cannot ascend to this level, then beat the retreat drum; even across hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, what can be done for you?
When the spirit of doubt arises and cannot be laid down, one has set out upon the path.

One must pin the two characters for "birth and death" upon one's forehead as if a fierce tiger were charging; if one does not walk straight home, one will surely lose one's life—how could one possibly stop?
In practicing the Way, apply your mind to a single koan alone; do not attempt to provide intellectual interpretations of all koans.

Even if you were able to interpret them, it would ultimately remain an interpretation rather than an awakening. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "This Dharma cannot be reached through thought, deliberation, or discrimination.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To use the calculating mind of discursive thought to fathom the Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the realm: it is like attempting to heat Mount Sumeru with a firefly; one will never succeed. Dongshan said:

"To attempt to study the profound mystery with the mind and intellect is much like heading west while facing east. Generally speaking, those who probe and analyze public cases must have blood beneath their skin and possess a sense of shame before they can succeed.

When practicing the method of cultivation, one must raise the *huatou* (critical phrase). One should simply maintain awareness of the doubt without being struck down by it; ultimately, there must be no second thought.
By all means, one must not cite proofs from the scriptures or allow the conscious mind (*vijñāna*) to be stirred. If the conscious mind is stirred, deluded thoughts will proliferate.
How then could one hope to achieve the severance of the path of words and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity? It would be impossible.
"The Way cannot be departed from for even a moment; that which can be departed from is not the Way. Spiritual practice (*kung-fu*) cannot be interrupted for even a moment;

that which can be interrupted is not spiritual practice. For one who truly investigates the truth, it is like fire burning upon one's eyebrows, or like saving one's own head from being set ablaze—how could there be leisure to give rise to thoughts of other matters?
As an ancient worthy said: 'It is as if one person were facing ten thousand enemies.'"

To meet face-to-face, there is no room for even a blink of an eye. You must understand that this statement is of the utmost importance for practicing the Way (*gongfu*). One must not fail to know this.
When practicing the Way, if you have not yet personally attained thorough penetration, you may only attend to your own affairs; you must not teach others.
It is like a person who has not yet reached the capital city yet speaks of the matters within it for others; not only does this deceive others, but it deceives oneself as well.
Listen!
In applying yourself to practice, do not dare to be indolent by day or night. For instance, when Master Ciming was about to fall asleep at night, he would use a leaden awl to prick himself.
He further said: "The ancients pursued the Way without eating or sleeping; who am I to be different?"
In ancient times, people drew a circle of lime; if their principles were not clear, their steps would not venture beyond the circle.
Nowadays, people indulge their whims and passions, wandering about without restraint, claiming this is "liveliness. This is truly laughable.
Through diligent practice, one may attain a state of lightness and ease, or experience a sudden awakening; however, these should not be taken as true enlightenment.
When Bo Shan was contemplating the phrase "The Boatman Monk left no trace," one day while reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*, he saw Zhaozhou’s instruction to a monk:
"Only when you meet someone three thousand miles away will you have it. At that moment, he suddenly lost his grip on his bag, as if letting go of a thousand catties of weight.

He carried this burden and claimed to have attained great enlightenment. Only upon meeting Baofang did it become as if a square block were being forced through a round hole; only then did he first feel shame and remorse.
If one does not meet a great spiritual friend after awakening, even if one attains ease and comfort, in the end it remains incomplete.
Baofang encouraged me with this verse: "When emptiness presses against emptiness, the merit is greatest; when existence pursues existence, the virtue remains slight.
To slander others while abiding in the natural principle of Kāśyapa is to lose what was gained at the very moment one found advantage.
This is a phrase for advancing beyond the hundred-foot pole; monks must examine it carefully. I once said to my students: "I have obtained Baofang’s [instruction]."
The two characters "unwilling" (bùkěn) are inexhaustible in their utility for practicing the Way.
One must not attempt to understand them through intellectual reasoning; rather, one must investigate them with stubborn persistence. Only then will the state of doubt (yíqíng) truly arise.
If one attempts to understand through intellectual reasoning, it will be nothing more than dry and hollow.
Not only will one fail to penetrate the matter of one's own self, but one will not even be able to give rise to doubt. It is like a person asking, "What is contained within this vessel?

If what is actually inside is not the object being pointed out, and that person takes what is not for what is, they will be unable to give rise to doubt; moreover, they will not even give rise to doubt at all.
To take that object for this object, and to take this object for that object—such is a mistaken understanding.
If one does not open the vessel and see it directly once, then one will never be able to distinguish them for the rest of one's life.
When practicing spiritual cultivation, one must not treat it as a matter of doing nothing. One must simply be resolute in seeking to clarify this principle.
If you treat it as a matter of doing nothing, you will spend your entire life merely as a person who does nothing; the great matter within the seam of your clothing will ultimately remain unresolved.
It is like a person searching for a lost object. If they find it, only then do they realize it;

if they do not find it, they simply leave it behind in a state of indifference and no longer have the intention to search. Even if the lost object were to appear before them, they would pass it by face-to-face, for they lack the intent to seek the object.

In practicing the Way, one must not understand it as being like the spark struck from flint or a flash of lightning. If you merely catch glimpses of light and shadow at the gateway of the mind, what benefit can that possibly bring?
You must attain direct realization and personal experience; only when you have seen it for yourself will it be achieved.
If you truly grasp the meaning, it is like seeing your own biological parents under the clear blue sky and bright daylight—the ultimate joy in this world.
Regarding the practice of cultivation, there is nothing more critical than this:
one must not engage in speculative calculation or discursive thought within the faculty of the intellect.

Such calculation prevents the practice from becoming a continuous whole and renders it impossible to give rise to the "doubt-mind" (*yiqing*). These four characters—"calculation," "speculation," "thought," and "discursive investigation"—obstruct right faith and hinder progress.
This is correct practice. Furthermore, it obstructs the eye of the Way; students must treat such [approaches] as if they were enemies before they can truly engage in the work of cultivation.
One must not take up the task at the point where the koan is raised. If one does so take it up, this is precisely what is meant by being muddled and superficial;
it is entirely incompatible with genuine investigation. You need only give rise to the spirit of doubt and strike through until it is thoroughly penetrated—without any taking up.
There is no place where one can take hold of it; it is like a pavilion in the sky, with openings on all seven sides and thorough access on all eight.
Otherwise, you will mistake the thief for your son and the slave for your master. As the ancient masters said: "Do not call the bridge of a donkey's saddle 'your father’s chin.
This is precisely what that means.
When practicing the Way, one must not seek someone else to explain it for you. If it were explained, it would ultimately remain another's realization;
it would have no bearing upon oneself. It is like a person asking the way to Chang'an: one may simply point out the direction, but one must not go on to inquire about the affairs of Chang'an itself.
Even if the other person explains every detail of Chang'an, it will ultimately remain something seen by another; it is not the personal realization of the one seeking the way.
Yes. If one does not practice with diligence but instead seeks for someone else to explain it for them, it is exactly the same.
As for practicing *gongfu*, it is not merely reciting a *kōan*. What connection can there be between such repetitive recitation and liberation?
Even if you recite until Maitreya descends to be born in this world, there will still be no connection. Why not recite the name of Amitābha Buddha? There is even greater benefit in that.
It is not that you need not contemplate at all; rather, it does not hinder you from raising each koan.

For instance, when contemplating the "Mu," you should give rise to the spirit of doubt precisely upon that "Mu. When contemplating the "Pine Tree," you should give rise to the spirit of doubt precisely upon the "Pine Tree.

When contemplating "Where does the One return? you should give rise to the spirit of doubt precisely upon "Where does the One return? Once the spirit of doubt has been fully aroused, [it will pervade] all ten directions.
The ten directions of the world are a single mass of doubt. With a body and mind that do not know their own parents, one’s entire being is this mass of doubt;
one does not know the ten directions of the world. Neither internal nor external, it rolls into a single lump.

One simply awaits that moment when the wooden band of the bucket bursts of its own accord, and upon meeting a true teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*) again, without even waiting for them to speak, the Great Matter will be completed. Only then...
Clapping his hands, he laughed aloud. "To turn back and contemplate a public case (gong'an) is much like a parrot learning to talk;
what relevance does it have? In practicing the work, one must not lose right mindfulness for even a moment.

If you lose that single thought of inquiry, you will inevitably flow into heterodox paths, forgetting and further forgetting until you do not return, like a person sitting in stillness who merely delights in a state of transparent clarity and pure, spotless serenity."
To regard this as performing Buddha-work is called losing right mindfulness; it is to fall into a state of stagnant stillness.
Or, to fixate upon a single entity that can speak and discourse, or can move and remain still, as being Buddha-work is called losing right mindfulness.
To recognize a "spirit" or to suppress the deluded mind so that the deluded mind does not arise, taking this to be Buddha-work, is called losing right mindfulness. Taking...
To suppress the deluded mind with the deluded mind is like pressing down grass with a stone. It is also like peeling the leaves of a plantain tree;

one layer after another, there is never a day when it reaches its end. Alternatively, if one contemplates the body and mind as being like empty space and fails to give rise to thoughts, making them like a blank wall, this is called losing right mindfulness.
Xuansha said: "If you attempt to concentrate the mind and collect the thoughts, withdrawing all phenomena back into emptiness..."
This is precisely the path of the nihilistic heretics, the dead whose spirits have not yet dispersed. In short, it is because one has lost right mindfulness.
When practicing *gongfu*, once the spirit of inquiry (*yiqing*) has been aroused, one must further break through it. If you cannot break through it, you must remain resolute.
This is true right mindfulness. One must arouse great courage and vigor; only by adding the word "utterly" (切) to "utterly" (切) can one succeed. Jingshan said:
"A man of great character who truly desires to bring this matter of great significance to its ultimate conclusion must, in one stroke, break through his own skin."
Be of a fiery nature and straighten your backbone. Do not follow the whims of others. Place that which you have long doubted upon the crown of your forehead.
At all times, act as if you owe someone ten thousand or a hundred thousand coins and are being pursued by creditors with nothing to repay them;
be as terrified of being shamed as one who fears disgrace, and be as urgent as one in the midst of an emergency, as busy as one in a state of panic, and as great as one who has attained the ultimate.
There is one matter that is truly interesting:
an evaluation of the ancient masters’ admonitions. Zhaozhou said:
"For thirty years I have not used my mind in a distracted manner; except for putting on clothes and eating meals, all else is using the mind in a distracted manner."

[The] Critique: It is not that he does not apply his mind; it is simply that he does not apply his mind in a distracted manner. This is what is meant by "place it in one spot, and there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
Zhaozhou said: "You need only investigate the principle and sit and watch. If after twenty or thirty years you still do not understand, cut off my head and take it with you!
[The] Critique: Why was Zhaozhou so desperate? Nevertheless, though this may be so, over the long course of years and months, one must seek that which is three...
It is rare to find one whose mind has remained unchanged for twenty years.
Zhaozhou said, "At eighteen, this old monk already knew how to break up the family and scatter the estate.
He also said, "In those days, I was driven by the twelve hours; now, I am able to drive the twelve hours. Commentary: In his home life, he made his living upon his estate.
Consider this: one who has squandered their family estate is driven by the twelve periods of the day.
Yet, when a monk suddenly asks, "What is the family estate? Bo Shan replies, "Once you have cast off this skin-sack, I shall tell you."
Zhaozhou said, "If you spend your entire life never leaving the monastic community and do not speak for five or ten years, no one will call you a mute.
Later on, even the Buddha will have nothing left to do with you. *Commentary:* Not speaking means that one’s mind is not distracted by external concerns.
However, if one does not investigate the principle within the "thread of the robe" (the immediate reality of one's own being), then one is far too distant from the truth.
National Teacher Shao of Tiantai said: "Even if one’s responses and discernments were like a cascading river, they would merely result in a perverted view.
If you value only the ability to respond and discern, what difficulty is there? I only fear it will be of no benefit to others."

This results in nothing but loss and error. [The] Critique: People of the present day learn enough to fill their bellies; they go back and forth with questions and answers, treating the Buddha-dharma as a mere plaything.
Not only is this of no benefit, it frequently leads to transgressions. Nowadays, people indulge in idle chatter as if it were the vehicle of the school.
When looking at the words of the ancients, how thick must their skin be?
The National Teacher said: "All you venerable elders have, from the past, engaged in much study—discriminating, debating, memorizing, and explaining principles.

Why, then, does your doubt not cease? When you hear the expedient means of the ancients, you fail to understand them at all. This is simply because there is much emptiness and little reality. [The Master] commented:
'Discriminating and memorizing both belong to conditioned conceptualization (*ālambana-vikalpa*). If the root of birth and death is not severed, how can it be?"*
Having realized the meaning of the ancients, it is said: "The subtle words remain stuck in the mind, becoming instead a field for discursive thought;
the ultimate reality resides right before one's eyes, yet turns instead into a realm of names and forms."
The National Teacher said: "Upādhyāya, you do not know how to see through it all at once from beneath your heels. Look into what kind of principle this is!
How many Dharma gates are there that could serve as objects for your doubts and seeking of liberation?

Only then will you realize that all those things you have studied until now are merely the root-source of birth and death, the livelihood within the realms of the aggregates. Therefore, the ancients said: "Seeing and hearing are not..."
"Deliverance is like the moon in the water. [Commentary: Who does not possess seeing, hearing, and mental deliberation? One must undergo a great transformation before it can be attained.
If it does not correspond with diligent practice, even if one descends from the Crystal Palace, there will ultimately be no connection.
As the ancient masters said: "Intellectual understanding entering the mind is like oil soaking into flour; there is never a time of emergence. This cannot be ignored.
Respectfully.
Chan Master Shaoyan said: "O worthy ones, today the National Master has extended this invitation solely for the purpose of you all clarifying the mind;
beyond this, there is no other principle. Have you all clarified the mind yet? Is it not simply a matter of words?"
When laughing and joking; when sitting in solemn silence; when seeking out spiritual teachers; when discussing the Way with fellow practitioners;
when gazing at mountains and playing by the water; and when the senses and ears are utterly stilled—is this your mind? Any understanding such as the above is entirely possessed by demonic spirits;
how could it be called "clarifying the mind"? Commentary: Neither speech is it, nor silence; neither seeing and hearing is it, nor is it apart from seeing and hearing.
"Even hearing is not it. How do you understand this? Let the practitioners of Chan today not be so confused.

Yanguan said: "Furthermore, there is another class of people who, apart from the delusive thoughts within their own bodies, separately recognize [the Buddha-nature] as pervading the worlds of the ten directions."
To claim that [the mind] contains the sun and moon and encompasses the great void, asserting it to be the original true mind, is also a calculation of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas);

it is not the realization of the enlightened mind. *Commentary:* This is called the "extreme emptiness" (prādeśika-śūnyatā) of the non-Buddhists. Furthermore, how could one possibly achieve the identity of body and mind, such that there is nothing remaining outside the body?
Nowadays, many Chan practitioners have never encountered a true teacher; they create their own masteries and mostly fall into this view.
Furthermore, O virtuous ones, do you understand? The mind has nothing that is "is," nor does it have anything that is "is not.
How could you possibly grasp or identify it? [Commentary: The preceding two types are illnesses; the fault lies in the two characters "grasping and identifying. This present section is the medicine:
simply by being without the grasping and identifying of "is" and "is not," the illness is cured.
Chan Master Rui Lu said: "In general, regarding the study of the Way, it is not necessarily the case that studying 'public cases' (hua) constitutes the study of the Way;

it is not necessarily the case that studying 'discriminating words' constitutes the study of the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying 'substitute words' constitutes the study of the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying 'alternative words' constitutes the study of the Way;

it is not necessarily the case that studying the breaking down of extraordinary phrases within the sutras and treatises constitutes the study of the Way; nor is it necessarily the case that one must break them down."
The extraordinary words of the Patriarchs are for the purpose of study.

If one studies in this manner, even if you attain mastery in all directions, should you still lack a point of realization within the Buddha-dharma, you are called a follower of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
Have you not heard that cleverness cannot withstand birth and death? How could dry wisdom escape the wheel of suffering? [Commentary: People of the present age are all like this.
This is truly what is meant by "discarding pure gold to pick up rubble.

One refuses to engage in genuine investigation and instead indulges in mere verbal samādhi—like Xiangyan, who would answer ten when asked one, or a hundred when asked ten. Is this not "thoroughly penetrating"? Yet within the Buddha-dharma, there is no point of realization;
one is utterly helpless regarding that single phrase of "before one's parents were born. This is the state of those studying nowadays.
Regarding the flow of words: tell me, what matters can these possibly resolve? Master Rulü said:
"If you are to study, you must study with genuine sincerity.
When walking, take it up while walking; when standing, take it up while standing; when sitting, take it up while sitting; when sleeping, take it up while sleeping."
Take it up. When speaking, take it up while speaking; when silent, take it up while silent; at all times of performing tasks, take it up while performing all tasks.
Since you are taking it up during such times as these, tell me: what person are you taking up? What phrase are you taking up?
At this point, you must have your own clear understanding before you can succeed. If it is not like this, [you will not].
To call this the conduct of the casual or hasty is to lack the ultimate principle. [The Master] commented:
"One must urgently investigate what kind of words are these words of inquiry, and who is this person who inquires.
If one does not investigate these words and does not recognize this person who inquires, it is called passing time in vain; it is not the study of Zen."
Bazhao said: "It is like a person walking along who suddenly encounters a ten-thousand-fathom deep pit ahead, while a wild fire presses from behind, with thorny brambles on both sides.
If he moves forward, he will fall into the pit; if he retreats..."
Then a wild fire burns your body; you turn over, and you are obstructed by a thicket of thorns. At such a time as this, how can you avoid it?
If you can avoid it, you possess a way to emerge from the situation. If you cannot avoid it, you are a man who has fallen and died.
Commentary: One must truly disregard danger and ruin before one can attain a state of total penetration. Should even the slightest doubt arise, one will lose both body and life.
This remark by Bāzāo is the most vital point of practice. Many students seek only intellectual understanding and fall into the traps of abstruse mysteries;
if they do not apply their attention here, it is said that they have lived their lives in vain.
