Yunmen said: "There is a certain kind of hollow scavenger who feeds on the spittle of others.

Having memorized a heap or a load of antiquated rubbish, he gallops about everywhere with the lips of a donkey and the mouth of a horse, boasting that he understands how to ask ten turns or five turns of questions.
Even if you were to question him from morning until night, for kalpas like this—have you ever even dreamed of it? *Commentary:* At that time, Yunmen was precisely...
Those who revile [the teaching] are but one or two individuals; nowadays, everyone is caught up in this clamor.
When have they ever investigated beneath their patched robes? Even when sitting for a brief moment, it is either dullness or distraction.
This is because they have a burden of entanglements in their bellies that they cannot spit out nor cut through. If one were a person of keen intelligence, as soon as they heard this—
"Ma-jü! Only by possessing great shame and remorse can one succeed.
Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying: "Brothers, do not easily let the time pass; you must be most careful.
The ancients had many entanglements with which they helped one another. For instance, Xuefeng said: 'The entire earth is your own self. [The text ends here.]
On a mountain path, seek the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses; in the bustling marketplace, recognize the Son of Heaven. Luopu said:
"When a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is fully contained within it. A lion on the tip of a single hair—its whole body is entirely there.
Grasp this and turn it over in your mind, contemplating it; as days and years pass, there will naturally come a point of entry. *Commentary:* These three passages.
These words lead you into the gate; they require that you be willing to enter. Otherwise, you will spend your entire life making a living inside a ghost cave.
If you can enter the gate, you will naturally become tranquil and still, seeing neither mountains, rivers, nor the great earth, nor even yourself.
To speak of "realizing" or "not realizing" is merely talk of two extremes.
Yunmen said: "When light does not penetrate through, there are two kinds of illness. First, being unenlightened in all places, as if there were something directly before one's face—this is it.
Furthermore, even if one has penetrated through so that all phenomena are empty, yet there is still a lingering sense as if something remains—this too is light not penetrating through.
Moreover, the Dharma-body also has two kinds of illness. Upon reaching the Dharma-body, if one does not forget the attachment to dharmas—this is it."
To see the self as still sitting within the vicinity of the *dharmakāya* is one [error]. Even if you manage to penetrate through to the *dharmakāya*, it is not permissible to let it pass unexamined.
If you scrutinize it carefully, what trace of vitality is there? It is also a sickness. Commentary:

This sickness lies entirely in making a livelihood upon the sphere of objective phenomena (*viṣaya-pramāṇa*). One has never cut it off, never penetrated through it, and never achieved a turning point.
He exhaled from his body. If one were to give rise to a separate or divergent thought here, there would be the possibility of becoming a demon or a malevolent spirit.
Xuan Sha said: "A bodhisattva who studies Prajñā must possess great capacity and great wisdom before they can succeed."
If one possesses wisdom, one can immediately escape and depart. Commentary:
For those of great capacity, hearing once brings a thousand awakenings, and they attain the Great Dharani. To speak the word "escape" is already a term of expedient means. Why is this so?
Because it has never been bound from the outset.

Xuansha said: "If one's faculties are dull and slow, one must exert oneself with diligence and hardship, forgetting fatigue day and night, losing sleep and missing meals, as if one had lost both parents.
Only by being so urgent and pressing throughout one's entire life can one further receive the support and guidance of others."
To investigate the reality down to the very marrow of one's bones is not difficult to grasp; how much more so now, who among us is truly capable of such study?
[The Master] commented: "All people throughout the entire world are capable, with the sole exception of those who are ignorant and lack the faculty of faith.
Even if Śākyamuni Buddha were to emit light and shake the earth, what could he do for them?"
Xuansha said: "Good man, do not merely memorize words and phrases; it is just like reciting a *dhāraṇī*.
You step forward with your feet while your mouth makes indistinct sounds, yet when someone seizes you and questions you, you have no way to escape.
You then become angry and say, 'The Master does not answer me! To study in such a manner is truly miserable. Do you understand?"
Commentary: To record the words of others is said to be like "mixed poison entering the heart," which obstructs right knowledge and vision.

Worldly scholars who memorize many texts find it difficult even to assimilate them; how much more so when it comes to investigating the supramundane Dharma? Would anyone be willing to consume the saliva and spittle of others?
Xuansha said: "There is a certain class of monks who sit upon rope-cots and claim to be 'good knowledge-holders' (śāstrins).

When questioned, they sway their bodies, wave their hands, roll their eyes, stick out their tongues, and stare blankly. My assessment is that such types are entirely possessed by demons and entirely afflicted by illness;
when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, they will inevitably end up in a state of turmoil."

Xuansha said: "Furthermore, there is another kind who speaks of 'bright and clear,' 'luminous consciousness,' and 'the nature of wisdom' that can see and hear, acting as a sovereign within the field of the five aggregates.
To act as a spiritual friend in such a manner greatly deceives people. Do you understand?"
I now ask you this: if you identify that which is bright and alert as your true self, why is it not bright and alert when you are dozing?
If it is not your true self when you are dozing, why does it exist when you are bright and alert?
Do you understand? This is called "mistaking a thief for one's own son"; it is the root of birth and death, a proliferation of deluded thoughts.
Commentary: This is a fellow who dabbles with his own spirit. Since he cannot master himself even when dozing off, how will he resolve it when birth and death arrive?
To spend a lifetime acting recklessly not only deceives others, but deceives oneself as well.
Xuansha said: "If you now wish to attain mastery over the field of the five aggregates, you must simply recognize your secret vajra-body.
The ancients told you: it is perfectly complete and all-pervasive, extending throughout the entire dharma-realm.

*Commentary:* The secret vajra-body is precisely that which is perfectly complete and all-pervasive, extending throughout the entire dharma-realm. It was clearly explained to you; you must [realize it].
Only when one forces the entire body into it can it be attained.
Xuansha said: "The Buddha-way is vast and open; there are no set paths. It is the gate of liberation that has no gate, the intent of the Way-person that has no intent.

It does not abide within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be subject to rising or sinking. To establish it is to deviate from the truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned creation."

Commentary: If one can realize this meaning, one attains Buddhahood on the spot without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort or practice—yet there is still the superfluous word "attain" (*cheng*).
Xuan Sha said: "To move is to give rise to the root of birth and death; to be still is to become intoxicated in the land of dullness and stupor. When movement and stillness are both...

To obliterate [all distinctions] is to fall into a state of voidness. To grasp both movement and stillness is to have a vague and superficial understanding of Buddha-nature. I evaluate this: practitioners often grow weary of movement and seek stillness;
having long remained in stillness, they again long for movement. One must raise the eyebrows and break through the conceptual nest of movement and stillness;
only then is it the true application of mind of a seeker of the Way.

Xuansha said: "One must face objects and confront circumstances like withered wood or cold ashes; when applying oneself to the moment, one does not fail to act appropriately. A mirror reflects all images without its radiance being disturbed; a bird flies through the air without mixing with the space or colors. Commentary: This teaching emphasizes the necessity of maintaining a state of non-attachment and equanimity amidst sensory phenomena. Like withered wood or cold ashes, the practitioner remains unresponsive to external stimuli, yet remains fully functional and responsive when required.

This is likened to a mirror that reflects myriad forms without its own luminosity being perturbed, or a bird soaring through the sky without becoming entangled with the space or colors it traverses. In these metaphors, the practitioner maintains a clear, unobstructed awareness that is neither distracted by nor fused with the phenomenal world. It is a state of dynamic stillness where action arises spontaneously and appropriately from a ground of total detachment.

Like withered wood or cold ashes, they possess no mind yet do not fail to act appropriately; for responding to things—how could this be compared to the state of extinguishing the intellect and freezing the heart?
That their radiance is undisturbed and that they are not confused by empty forms and colors—what does this have to do with me?
What concern is it to me?
Xuansha said: "Therefore, throughout the ten directions there are no images; within the three realms, all activity is cut off.

One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor does one dwell in the intention of the middle way. Within this, even a hair’s breadth cannot be fully described; to do so would be to become a retainer of the Mara King.

The 'before the phrase' and 'after the phrase' are the difficult points for students. Thus, when a single phrase accords with the Way, the eighty thousand gates are forever severed from birth and death."
Commentary: The essence of these words lies in a single phrase that encompasses the eighty-four thousand gates.

Throughout the ten directions of the world, there is not the slightest bit of vacancy, not the slightest bit of reflection, and not the slightest bit of trace. It may be called radiantly brilliant and vibrantly alive;
Buddhas, patriarchs, and sentient beings have no place to rest, and even the two characters for "birth and death" find no footing. Who is it that speaks thus?

Xuansha said: "Even if it were like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—unimpaired by being struck and undispersed by touching the waves—it is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death.
*Commentary:* If a practitioner of seated meditation does not reach such a state, even if they do reach it, it is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. One must seek for oneself...
A way out is finally found.
Xuansha said: "Where a man of the Way proceeds, it is like fire melting ice; it never turns back into ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring..."
There is no momentum for returning; therefore, it will not stay within its cage, and though called, it does not turn its head back.

The ancient sages made no arrangements, and thus to this day there is no fixed location. *Commentary:* The mind of a practitioner ought to be like this. Simply take this passage and rub it thoroughly;
then, naturally, you will find it effortless. Not even a trace of attachment should remain. If you attempt to settle the conscious mind within it, you will fail.
This is what is meant by the saying: "If the ground is not true, the fruit will be circuitous. Xueyan said: "People of the present age do not awaken to the principle within this;

they recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust, becoming stained and attached everywhere, bound and fettered at every turn. Even if they were to awaken, the realms of sensory objects would remain chaotic and the names and forms unreal. *Commentary:* This passage critiques the failure to realize the fundamental nature of reality while remaining entangled in the phenomena of the mundane world. It emphasizes that without a true foundation in the Dharma, spiritual cultivation inevitably leads to a distorted result.

The "ground" refers to one's initial resolve and the purity of one's practice; if these are lacking, the "fruit"—the realization of enlightenment—will be indirect and obscured. Xueyan’s observation highlights the common error of practitioners who, failing to penetrate the core truth, allow their minds to be distracted and defiled by external conditions. Consequently, even when moments of insight occur, they are overwhelmed by the proliferation of sensory data and the unreality of conventional designations, preventing the attainment of stable liberation. Thus, the essential point is that true awakening must arise from a genuine and unwavering commitment to the Way.
Remaining attached to sensory objects, one is bound at every turn; this is simply because one’s investigation of the mind is not earnest, and thus the life-root remains unsevered, refusing to die.
A true student of the Way is like one passing through a land of pestilential poison: not even a single drop of water may be touched.
He had just attained a thorough realization.
Xuansha said: "If you intend to concentrate the mind and withdraw the thoughts, to subsume phenomena into emptiness; to close your eyes and hide your gaze;
and as soon as a thought arises, to immediately break it down, or as soon as a subtle perception emerges, to immediately suppress it—such a view is precisely falling [into error]."
These are the "void-and-lost" heterodox practitioners—dead men whose spirits have not yet dispersed. In a state of dark obscurity, they are without awareness or cognition;

they plug their ears and steal the bell, merely deceiving themselves in vain. Commentary: Their ailment lies in failing to give rise to the spirit of doubt (*yiqing*), failing to investigate the public case (*gongan*), and refusing to allow the whole body to enter into principle.
They merely attempt to suppress the conscious mind. Even if it becomes clear and tranquil, in the end, it is but life.
If the roots are not severed, one will ultimately not be a person who practices the Way.
Xuansha said: "O worthy one, do not merely remain attached to the net of love for birth and death; you will be bound away by the karma of good and evil."

There is no portion of liberation. Even if you refine yourself until body and mind become like empty space, even if you reach the state of brilliant clarity that is profound and unshakable, you have not escaped the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness).
The ancients called this "like a rushing torrent; because the flow is so swift, one does not perceive it, falsely taking it for tranquility.
My assessment: as long as the conscious mind is not severed, even if you refine body and mind until they are like empty space, you will ultimately be overcome by evil.
Karma drags one away; that state which is brilliant, lucid, and unmoving is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). How can one escape birth and death?
In short, if one does not thoroughly investigate the Great Principle, everything is entirely false and illusory.

Xuansha said: "To practice in such a manner, one will never escape the cycle of saṃsāra; as before, one will continue to be driven by it. Therefore it is said: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Even the fruits and rewards of the Three Vehicles are thus to be feared. Without the Eye of the Way, there is no ultimate realization.
*Commentary:* Taking these several preceding passages of Dharma speech together, none of them constitute the ultimate; they pertain only to the Three Vehicles.

"Even if a practitioner performs the myriad practices of the six pāramitās, they are all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; at the ground of ultimate reality, they have no connection whatsoever.
Jìngshān said: 'In the present age, there is a kind of outsider who, because their own eyes are not clear, merely teaches others to pursue death with frantic intensity.'"
"Resting in the ground of the objective, resting and ceasing. If you rest and cease in this manner, even when a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, you will still be unable to rest;

it will only cause your mind to become increasingly bewildered and distressed. Commentary: If you are unwilling to give rise to the state of doubt (*yiqing*), then the life-root (*minggen*) will not be severed.

Since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not yet severed, one neither comes to rest nor departs; one cannot even find cessation. These very two characters, "rest" and "cessation," are the very root of birth and death.
Even through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, there will ultimately be no day of final resolution.
Jingshan said: "There is another class of people who instruct others to follow conditions while maintaining control, to forget emotions and practice silent illumination.
Yet as they illuminate again and again, and carry this practice along with them, their confusion and distress only increase further, with no end in sight. [Commentary:

Since there is already a mind that can maintain control and an object-field that is being illuminated, the duality of subject and object stands opposed; how could this be anything other than delusion? If one takes such a deluded mind as the basis for investigation, [how can one ever attain liberation?]"
One will then find no mastery over one's own mind; it is simply necessary to cut off both ends and let neither subject nor object stand.
Then, that which has been obstructing the chest will fall away like the bottom of a bucket.
Jingshan said: "Furthermore, there is another class of people who teach others not to concern themselves with any matters, but simply to rest in this way.
When they have come to such a state of resting that emotional thoughts do not arise, it is not a state of blank unconsciousness;
rather, it is truly alert and vivid. This kind of person is even more harmful; they blind the eyes of others. This is no small matter. [The author] comments: It is merely...
To reach a state of being fully alert and clearly discerning—this is the Dharma of confronting stillness; is it not the practice of investigation?
If one investigates, it is because one directly desires to realize the Great Matter. Since you do not act in this way, are you not, indeed, a source of harm?
Jingshan said: "Regardless of whether one is a long-standing practitioner or a senior master, if you wish for true stillness, you must shatter the mind of birth and death.
Do not rely on the practice of 'gongfu. Once the mind of birth and death is shattered, there is natural stillness. *Commentary:* Only when the spirit of doubt (*yiqing*) can be fully aroused.
Thus, the mind of birth and death is coagulated in a single place; when the state of doubt is shattered, the mind of birth and death is shattered.
At this point of shattering, one seeks its moving aspect, but it is utterly unfindable.
When the state of doubt (*yiqing*) fails to arise, one is shown the admonition to apply oneself to the practice of *gongfu*.
If doubt does not arise, one then desires to seek out written characters and count the ink-strokes, scrutinizing texts to extensively seek intellectual understanding.
One attempts to thread the teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs onto a single string, stamping them all with a single seal to fix them in place. As soon as—

To take up a koan and attempt to understand it through intellectual reasoning, failing to give rise to the spirit of doubt regarding the original subject of inquiry, and feeling displeasure when confronted with difficult questions from others—this is the mind of arising and ceasing; it is not Chan.

Sometimes responding to sounds with gestures—raising a finger, clenching a fist, or swiftly drawing characters to write verses for instruction—they lead people to investigate the matter, which indeed possesses a certain flavor.
They claim to have attained the great gate of enlightenment, yet they do not realize that their state of doubt has failed to arise;
all such actions are merely the workings of the conscious mind. If one were willing to recognize this error in a single thought and let go of everything entirely, one should seek out a true teacher.
This may serve as an entry point; otherwise, the mind of birth and cessation will prevail. If this continues for long, one will become possessed by demons, which is nearly impossible to remedy.

When practicing the *kung-an* (koan), if doubt (*yiqing*) does not arise and one instead develops a sense of weary detachment toward sensory objects and conditions, one will merely delight in reaching a state of quietude and emptiness.
When a person sits, they may feel strength and feel that there is some sense of purpose. Yet, as soon as they encounter even the slightest movement, the mind becomes displeased;
this is the mind of arising and ceasing, not Chan. After sitting for a long time, one then accords with the state of stillness, becoming dark and oblivious, transcending both extremes and relativity.
Even if one attains such meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) and fixes the mind so it does not move, how is this different from the various vehicles of the Lesser Vehicle?
This is what makes them different. Whenever they encounter external conditions, they lack self-mastery; upon hearing sounds or seeing forms, they give rise to fear and dread.
Because of this fear and dread, Māra gains the opportunity; because of Māra’s power, they perform all manner of unwholesome deeds.
Thus, their lifelong cultivation yields no benefit at all, for it all stems from their initial improper application of mind and the arising of unwholesome doubt, leading them to refuse to see others.

Unwilling to trust others, you forcibly assume mastery over a place of stillness and silence. Even if you encounter a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), you refuse to recognize your error for even a single thought-moment.
Though a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, what can they do for you?

When practicing the method of cultivation, if the great doubt (*sīmā*) does not arise, you must suppress the mind of emotional consciousness and delusive thoughts, ensuring that the deluded mind does not stir.
When you reach the state where no thoughts arise, the mind becomes limpid and profoundly still—pure and free from even a single speck of defilement.

Yet, at this point, the root-source of this conscious mind remains ultimately unbroken. You continue to apply effort and seek understanding within this state of limpidity and spotless purity; however, as soon as you encounter someone pointing it out...
It strikes at the painful spot, like pressing down on a gourd upon water; this is the mind of arising and ceasing, not dhyāna.
This is because you initially refused to investigate the *huatou* (critical phrase) and give rise to the state of doubt (*yiqing*).

Even if you could forcibly suppress the body and mind so they do not arise—like grass pressed down by a stone—if you were to cause the consciousness-mind (*shixin*) to die out and fall into annihilation, you would precisely be falling into the path of the nihilistic heretics. If...
It does not cease and depart; rather, when encountering objective conditions, it immediately gives rise to the conscious mind.

Within the state of profound stillness and absolute purity, one then forms a "sacred understanding," claiming for oneself that one has attained the gate of great enlightenment. If one indulges in this, one becomes mad; if one clings to it, one becomes a demon.
Amidst worldly dharmas, such delusion and ignorance give rise to deep calamity, causing others to lose their faith and obstructing the path to Bodhi.
When practicing the cultivation of the Way, if the spirit of doubt (*sīqíng*) does not arise, one should empty away both the body-mind and the vessel-world (*jìjiè*).

One empties until reaching a state where there is nothing to grasp or maintain, and no place of reliance. One sees neither body nor mind, nor does one see the world. It is neither internal nor external;
it is all, in its entirety, a single void. To say that this void is Chan, and that being able to attain this void is to be a Buddha—this is practice as well.
"Emptiness! Sitting is also emptiness; coming and going are empty. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are like moving through the midst of empty space.
This is the mind of arising and ceasing; it is not Chan. If you do not attach to it, it becomes a dull emptiness—dark and devoid of awareness. If you do attach to it, it becomes a demonic state.

You may claim for yourself that you have attained a great gate of enlightenment, yet you do not realize that this has no connection whatsoever with the practice of Zen. If you are truly such a person..."
A Chan practitioner must give rise to the great doubt; a single phrase of the meditation topic is like a sky-reaching long sword—anyone who strikes its edge will immediately lose their life.
If it is not so, even if you manage to attain a state where not a single thought arises, this is merely called "emptiness" or "knowing nothing"—is this not the ultimate? It is not.
When practicing the cultivation of the Way, if the spirit of doubt (yiqing) does not arise, one then begins to speculate with the conscious mind, recklessly interpreting ancient kōans.
One claims they represent the "total presentation" (quanti), or the "partial presentation" (banti); one claims they point "upward," or that they point "downward."
"This is the ruler; this is the subject. These are words of simultaneous inclusion; these are words of plain reality.

One claims one's own insight is beyond the reach of others, yet even if one can explain every point with logical reasoning, it is merely sharing a single breath with the ancients—this is a mind of arising and ceasing, not Chan.
Little do they realize that every word and every phrase of the ancients is like chewing a ball of cotton wool: it causes people to be unable to swallow it.
If you cannot spit it out, how could you possibly grant people so many pathways of intellectual understanding and provoke their conscious minds?
If your state of doubt can be aroused, enter wholeheartedly and press through these pathways of understanding and the conscious mind.
Before you even die, it will naturally settle into a state of profound stillness.
When practicing meditation, if the great doubt (*sīmā*) does not arise, look through and see through the body and mind; they are entirely composed of false conditions.
Within them, there is naturally one thing that comes and goes, capable of both motion and stillness, formless and signless. It emits light and shakes the earth at the gates of the six sense organs;
when dispersed, it pervades the entire dharma-realm; when withdrawn, not even a speck of dust remains. Here, recognize it once and for all.

If one remains settled in meditation, refuses to give rise to the spirit of doubt, and refuses to investigate and examine, claiming instead to be "one who has finished with affairs," this is merely the mind of birth and death, not Chan.
Little do they realize that as long as the mind of birth and death is not shattered, taking such things to be a source of pleasure is precisely playing with the *vijñāna* (consciousness).
Once the light of the eyes falls to the ground [at death], one will be unable to act as master; one will be led away by the *vijñāna*, following it wherever it drags one along.
When one departs to receive the retribution of karma, if one’s wholesome karma is abundant, one will be born among humans or in the heavens.

Yet, when the four signs and five decays approach and press upon one, one immediately claims that the Buddha-dharma lacks spiritual efficacy. Due to this slander of the Dharma, one falls into the realms of hell or hungry ghosts.
Even after emerging from there, one would not know how many kalpas have passed. Viewed in this light, the practice of Zen requires absolute commitment.
When one observes people—if they take themselves as the sovereign master, they find it entirely useless for their practice.

If the spirit of doubt cannot be aroused while performing spiritual work, they simply fixate on the notion that the eye can see, the ear can hear, the tongue can speak, the nose can smell, the hands can grasp, and the feet can run;
they then identify this as their own singular, numinous true nature. Thus they proceed...
This is measuring; it is called a gate of awakening. When meeting people, one stares with bulging eyes and pricked ears, using finger-pointing and foot-kicking as the Buddha-dharma.
This is the mind of arising and ceasing; it is not Chan. The ancients called it being like one who has fallen into a fit of epilepsy.
They also said it is like playing with "ghost-eyes" upon a curved armrest chair. One plays with them and plays with them until—
When the four great elements disperse, it cannot be taken away by play. Furthermore, there is a class of people with evil views who consider this to be extraordinary;

they pass it down from generation to generation and receive offerings from others. Shameless and without remorse, whenever they encounter someone asking about the Dharma, they let out a great shout and break into a loud laugh.
Little do they realize that they have never investigated the matter from the beginning, and their life-root remains unsevered, even as they wander about.
"Virtuous deeds are all the work of Māra; they are not ultimate.

When practicing *gongfu*, if doubt (*yiqing*) does not arise, one may then desire to perform conditioned meritorious practices (*saṃskṛta-kriyā*), or seek liberation, or practice asceticism—such as not using a stove in winter or a fan in summer, or when someone comes to beg for clothing, immediately stripping off one's entire body and gladly enduring it.
To die of cold is called liberation. When people come to beg for food, they themselves do not eat, willingly accepting death by starvation;
this is called liberation. There are many other such varieties that cannot be described in detail. Generally speaking, these are all driven by a superior mind that deceives the ignorant.
Those who are ignorant regard them as living Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, [serving] them for the rest of their lives.

To serve and make offerings [to a Buddha] is, within the Buddhist precepts, called the karma of improper conduct (*akuśala-vinaya*). Although one may be observing the precepts, one incurs transgressions at every step.
Furthermore, there are those who burn their bodies or set their arms on fire, prostrating to the Buddha and seeking repentance, claiming this to be their daily practice (*kōko*).

While such acts may be considered good deeds within worldly conventions, what is to be gained from them in the context of investigating the essence of the Way? As the ancient masters said: [text follows].
He said: "By all means, do not seek within the realm of sensory stimuli and mental objects (*ālambana*).

To say that prostrating to the Buddha is a realm of stimuli and objects, or that seeking repentance is a realm of stimuli and objects—indeed, all wholesome matters within the Buddha-dharma are realms of stimuli and objects. This does not mean I am teaching you not to perform these various wholesome deeds;
rather, it is simply that you must focus your mind on one point. Then, all these wholesome deeds will be able to assist in their manifestation and nurture your roots of goodness."
One day, his eye of the Way suddenly opened; he realized that burning incense and sweeping the floor are themselves acts of Buddha-work.

When practicing the kōan, if doubt does not arise and one wishes instead to be dissolute, or wishes to be merely frivolous—singing and dancing upon meeting people, or finding joy and amusement for oneself, or reciting poetry and chatting by the water or beneath the trees, or in the marketplace— [The text continues: ...or in the market...
Wandering aimlessly through the streets and lanes like a well-dwelling dog, he claims to be one who has settled his affairs.

When he sees a spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra) opening a monastic community, establishing rules and guidelines, or engaging in sitting meditation, reciting the Buddha’s name, or performing any virtuous deeds, he slaps his hands in loud laughter, giving rise to a mind of contempt and a mind of slanderous irreverence.
Unable to practice the Path himself, he obstructs others from practicing the Path; unable to... [complete the sentence as necessary].

[He claims to] recite sutras and perform repentance rituals, yet he obstructs others from reciting sutras and performing repentance rituals. He himself cannot practice Chan meditation, yet he obstructs others from practicing Chan meditation.

He himself cannot establish monastic communities, yet he obstructs others from establishing monastic communities. He himself cannot preach the Dharma, yet he obstructs others from preaching the Dharma.
Whenever a true spiritual friend appears in the world, he poses several difficult questions; before the assembly of devas and humans, he manages to provide one extra answer.
He asks one more question, lets out a shout, and gives a slap. When a true teacher (Sanskrit: *kalyāṇamitra*) sees him acting like a ghostly plaything, he may simply ignore him.
Then that person tells others, "This true teacher does not understand this principle.
Alas! Alas! This is merely the victory of the mind of arising and ceasing; if it persists, one will be drawn into the path of demons (*māra*), creating inexhaustible depths of suffering.
Calamity! Having exhausted the blessings received from Mara, one falls into the Avīci Hell. Though this was a virtuous cause, it has brought about an evil fruit—how tragic!

When practicing *gongfu*, if doubt (*yi-qing*) does not arise, one realizes that such a state is no different from that of the common crowd; every movement and gesture becomes inconvenient, and one feels excessively constrained.
It was too chaotic and distracting, so he wished to go live in quiet seclusion in the deep mountains where there were no people, or perhaps to live in quiet seclusion within a single room.

At first, he would forcibly take charge, closing his eyes and concentrating his mind, sitting in the full lotus posture with palms joined, practicing with great rigidity for a year or two, or a month or two, yet he saw no progress. Furthermore, there was another class who sat...
Within two or three days, they become unable to sit still; they may read books, or act with idle dissipation, or compose gāthās and poems, or shut their doors to sleep.
Outwardly they manifest dignified decorum, yet inwardly they have become vulgar. Furthermore, there is a class of wicked youths who lack a sense of shame and do not believe in cause and effect;
they secretly indulge in greed and desire, speaking and acting as they please whenever they encounter others, deceiving and lying.
Ignorant, they claim, "I have seen a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra); I have attained the dharmas of a superior person," in order to cause the ignorant to believe and accept this.
They establish friendly relations with them, or form spiritual bonds as fellow practitioners, or recruit them as disciples. Thus, the superior leads and the inferior follows.
Not realizing their own faults, they refuse to reflect upon themselves and refuse to see others; they falsely exalt themselves until they commit great falsehoods.
Such people are truly to be pitied. In this age, they loathe the great assembly and seek out private chambers—how can one not feel a chill in one's heart?
If you are a true student of the Way, be careful never to give rise to such thoughts; it is precisely when you are among the multitude that you should engage in inquiry.
Investigate! Both you and I must remain vigilant. Even if you do not awaken to the Way, you will certainly never fall into such a state.
Students must not fail to be on guard.
These words of warning are intended to inspire the arising of the spirit of doubt.

When practicing the Way, if the great doubt can be aroused and one accords with the principle of the Dharmakāya, one will see the entire earth as a brilliant, pure radiance, without the slightest obstruction.
At that point, one desires to take charge of this matter and refuses to let go, remaining seated at the limit of the Dharmakāya’s measure.
Because of this, the life-root is not severed; within the Dharmakāya, there appears to be a "view" and an appearance of "reception."
To employ [such methods] is, in fact, entirely the product of one's own conceptualization. The ancients called this "the phrase that separates the body.

As long as the life-root (*mūla*) is not severed, the entire person is afflicted by illness; this is not Chan. At this point, one must simply drive oneself wholeheartedly into it and take up this great matter, yet remain unaware of even one who takes it up.
As the ancient worthy said: "Letting go at the precipice, one spontaneously consents to take it up; there is no..."
Later, he revived once more. One cannot deceive the Sovereign. If the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed, it is entirely the mind of arising and ceasing.
If the life-root is severed and one does not know how to turn the body or exhale, such a person is called a "corpse who has fallen dead.
Is this not the ultimate? This principle is not difficult to understand; it is simply that the practitioner is unwilling to see a true teacher. If one encounters a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend)...
When you strike the vital point, you will immediately know where to return. If this is not yet so, then you shall lie prostrate as a corpse ten thousand *li* away.
When practicing the work, if the spirit of doubt can be aroused, it will accord with the principle of the Dharma-body.

It stirs up the turbid world, and one attains a state of enjoyment where waves surge and billows roll. If the practitioner becomes addicted to this enjoyment, they will be unable to push forward or restrain themselves.
Step back! Because of this, you cannot penetrate fully. It is like a poor man who encounters a mountain of solid gold;
he clearly and vividly knows it is gold, yet he cannot take it in his hand and use it. The ancients called such a person a "man guarding a treasure.
His entire being is an illness; this is not Chan. Reaching this point, you must simply disregard life and death before you can succeed.
It is in accord with the Dharma. As the Celestial Youth said, "The entire Dharma-realm is made into a single meal. With nostrils hanging down, one truly knows the satisfaction of thorough study.
If you do not have your nostrils hanging down, it is like sitting by the side of a grain basket and starving to death, or dying of thirst in the midst of the great ocean.
What matters can such a person ever resolve? Therefore it is said: "After awakening, one must simply meet people," as was the case with the ancient masters who attained realization.
Later, when one encounters a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they possess great exemplary character.

Truly, when pure light shines upon the eyes, is this not because the water is clear, the pearl is lustrous, the wind is fresh, and the moon is white?

such a state occurs in an instant—is this not the ultimate? Those who lack understanding simply let go of the doubt-mind and refuse to investigate further. By themselves—

To use the conscious mind for conjecture is for the whole body to be diseased; this is not Chan.

Because one’s entry into principle is not deep and one turns back too soon, even if there is profound understanding, it does not yield practical utility. Even if one attains the "live word" (*huoju*), one should properly remain by the waterside or beneath the forest trees.
Cultivate yourself with restraint and modesty. By no means should you be impetuous, seeking to become a teacher, or recklessly exalting yourself.
You must understand that when you first apply your mind and the state of doubt arises and coalesces into a single mass, you should simply wait for it to burst open of its own accord.
Only then can one truly begin to experience [the Dharma]. Otherwise, if you let go of your doubts as soon as you encounter some slight logical reasoning, you will certainly not die here;
you will certainly not be thoroughly penetrated. Your entire life will pass in vain; you will have the reputation of practicing Chan, but lack the reality of practicing Chan.
Even if you were to enter the marketplace and extend a helping hand, it would still be better to further meet a great *kalyāṇamitra*. As for such a *kalyāṇamitra*:
This is a great king of physicians, able to cure grave illnesses; this is a great donor, able to bestow according to one's wishes.
One must by no means give rise to thoughts of self-satisfaction. If one does not wish to see others, know that such refusal to see others stems from clinging to one's own views;
in the midst of dhyāna, there is no greater grave illness than this.

his movements must be composed and full of circumspection. Do not vainly use your intellectual views to falsely distinguish between the distant and the intimate. Press until doubt is crushed to pieces.

"Grabbing the tiger by its whiskers. When asked, "What is it like on the road to the Terrace? he pointed distantly toward the village ahead and said, "Go straight on.

Red. A land of lotus flowers with jeweled ponds and golden ground; ten thousand streams all return within the range of a single glance. Within this glance, empty this thought.

Before the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, the deep waters are still and clear; across the expanse of empty sky, idle clouds drift in fragments.

one must not fall into the five aggregates or external demons as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Once one initially becomes attached, it can no longer be destroyed. This very delusive thought is the root and core of Māra.
If its root is not eliminated, how can one hope to crush its branches and leaves so that they do not arise? At worst, this only serves to nourish them.

The mind that illuminates must have an object that is observed and illuminated. When subject and object stand in opposition, how can this be anything other than delusion?
Therefore, the Chan school says: "Treading alone upon the Great Way, there is no objective realm outside the mind.

By merging the ten directions of the world, as well as one's own body and mind, into a single whole, and cutting off both extremes, one finally attains the entrance. As for the path leading upward, it is even more so.
You must examine this for yourself; otherwise, it is entirely the livelihood of ghosts. How can such things be spoken of as being on the same level as cultivation and realization?
If one is indeed so crude as not to reach this point, it is called self-deception. Such people are truly to be pitied.
"Is it not worthy of being recorded? Nanyue said: 'Cultivation and realization are indeed not absent, yet defilement is impossible.
This very cultivation that is undefiled may be called perfect cultivation; can one still apply the word 'cultivation' to it?
This very realization that is undefiled may be called perfect realization; can one still apply the word 'realization' to it? In this way, one cultivates all day long."

Yet there is no cultivation. Sweeping the ground and burning incense are all immeasurable Buddha-activities; how could these ever be abandoned? It is simply that one does not cling to cultivation or realization.

Even at the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), there is still no effortful practice (*anābhoga-caryā*); how much more so at the tenth stage? This extends even to the preaching of the Dharma by those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Like rain or clouds, such [views] were still rebuked by Nanquan as being utterly at odds with the Way; how much more so, then, can one compare the contemplative insight of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) with the School of the Patriarchs to determine their relative superiority? Is that even permissible?
Ten Verses on the Instruction for Studying Chan To study Chan, one must be an iron man;
One need not concern oneself with time or limits. Biting down firmly upon the gate of the teeth, One should resolve only to accomplish the Great Matter.
In a cauldron of fierce fire and boiling oil, Even empty space is boiled until it is soft.
Suddenly one morning, turning it over, Let go of the thousand-pound weight;
do not debate the length of time spent in Zen. Do not consort with worldly conditions;
Raising the two eyebrows, the void runs upside down. Mount Sumeru is ground to dust; At this very moment, pursue that which is inherently possessed.
When the molten gold of raw iron flows forth, one finally escapes former faults;
in practicing Zen, do not be reckless. One’s conduct must be examined through antiquity;
let the single string of the lute be kept in mind so as not to suffer on the forked paths. Shatter the barrier of Huanglong; cast aside Yunmen’s "Universal."
This dilapidated monk has never stepped outside his door to practice Chan;
he possesses no mastery over his own mind. He simply requires that his heart remain unaltered:
though the myriad phenomena and the dust of worldly toil swirl about him, who cares? Firm and resilient enough to support the heavens, brave and decisive enough to drain the sea.
Though you have not yet reached the ultimate end, take it for granted that your future path lies ahead.
When practicing Chan, you must be discerning; do not calculate your progress like a construction project.
If there is a handle, grab it; if there is no handle, grab the precedent. Do not concern yourself with Buddhas or Patriarchs; what need is there to worry about sutras and gāthās?
Swallow it all at once; only when the mind is empty does one pass the examination.
When Zen study awakens right faith, the palace of Māra trembles. A flake of snow enters a red furnace;
walking naked through white blades, seek only the path of life, and do not let yourself be submerged in stagnant death.
The Great San Pass suddenly opens; The inverted horse-shoulder seal of Vairocana—do not toy with it while practicing Zen.
In a flash, time has changed; The ultimate principle and its profound mysteries are like the gilding and drilling of the Qin era.
Alas! The mind of a man of integrity— When the hand is applied, one must judge for oneself.
How much of a hundred years can there be? Do not wait until the moment of departure to practice Zen in a state of confusion.
There is no skill or clumsiness here; a single thought-moment prizes transcendence.
Recognize the reflection upon the finger, then directly probe for the moon at the edge of the sky. Split open the chest to see the heart; scrape away the fur to reveal the blood.
I have clearly set this forth for you; if you do not understand, to whom can you speak?
You must practice Zen while it is still early; do not wait until your years are spent. When the ears are deaf and the eyes grow dim, what is present in the morning may be lost by evening.
All that was most joyful in one’s life—by the time one reaches this point, it has all fallen into ruin.
The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not manifold; it requires only that you realize it now.

Do not practice meditation by trying to rectify delusions; to try to rectify delusions still constitutes an obstruction. It is like one who wishes to obtain flowers—what does it matter if the waves surge?
The ultimate essence is devoid of even a speck of dust; what form, then, could a deluded mind have?
Respectfully addressed to those who practice Zen meditation: this gate is truly worthy of admiration.
